newsitem.title: FRANCE: Chirac to say French not conservative, but dynamic.
newsitem.headline: Chirac to say French not conservative, but dynamic.

text.p: French President Jacques Chirac, criticised during his last television appearance for stressing the "conservatism" of his fellow-citizens, will highlight their dynamism in a New Year address on Tuesday, Le Monde said.

The newspaper said the centre-right president, unpopular like his prime minister Alain Juppe, will deliver an upbeat message focusing on his "determination" and "hope", and will reaffirm his confidence in austerity policies despite rising unemployment.
Chirac's office was unavailable for comment on the newspaper report ahead of his address, being broadcast at 2000 (1900 GMT).
The business daily Les Echos said Chirac would tell the French that his policies would begin to bear fruit in the New Year.
It will the head of state's second New Year message since his election in mid-1995, and his second appearance on television in less than a month.

His appeals for understanding of austerity policies in a lengthy interview on December 12 failed to lift his low popularity significantly, with he and Juppe rising only slightly in recent opinion polls.
Opposition Socialists derided Chirac as apparently powerless given his criticism of the French for resisting many of his reforms.
Le Monde said Chirac would argue that the French economy had been boosted by measures pushed through by the government, including tax and welfare reforms.

"Chirac wants to show that he does not see France as a country which has to be dragged like a ball and chain, but as a country which has the assets to face up to globalisation and the new rules of economic competition," wrote Le Monde.
French unemployment hit a record 12.7 percent in November, resuming its steady rise after a surprise drop in October, and economists said the peak was still some way off.
The number of unemployed rose by 20,700 last month, after a 12,000 decline in October, to reach 3,121,500 after adjustment for seasonal variations, the Labour Ministry said on Monday.
This rise pushed the jobless rate up from 12.6 percent of the workforce in October.

For the government, languishing at record lows in opinion polls, the figures make its pledge to cut unemployment ever harder to fulfil as it tries to rein in spending to meet deficit criteria for joining a single European currency in 1999.
